title: How to Keep a Consistent Writing Style in Claude Projects
body_md:
![support.anthropic.com official page screenshot](https://afroditena.github.io/mattress-checklist-android/assets/img/how-to-keep-a-consistent-writing-style-in-claude-projects/1.png)
*Screenshot of support.anthropic.com ([source](https://support.anthropic.com/en/articles/10185728-understanding-claude-s-personalization-features))*

One way to get more consistent writing out of Claude is to stop re-explaining your voice in every chat and move those rules into a Project. Project instructions tell Claude the context and requirements for a particular project, and they only apply to chats inside that project - so every new conversation in that workspace starts with your style rules already loaded. Pair that with uploaded samples of your own writing and, optionally, account-level instructions or a skill, and the output gets steadier over time.

Here's the setup, start to finish.

## What You'll Need

![anthropic.com official page screenshot](https://afroditena.github.io/mattress-checklist-android/assets/img/how-to-keep-a-consistent-writing-style-in-claude-projects/2.png)
*Screenshot of anthropic.com ([source](https://www.anthropic.com/news/styles))*

- A Claude account. Anthropic's help center says projects are available to all users, including those with free Claude accounts, and free users can create a maximum of five projects ([source](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/9519177-how-can-i-create-and-manage-projects)), and the [pricing page](https://claude.com/pricing) lists Projects as "Up to 5" on Free. Anthropic's pricing table is confusing here - it markets "unlimited projects" as a Pro benefit, so read the help center as the operative source. Paid plans add more usage and features.
- 3–5 pieces of writing you're genuinely happy with (published posts, newsletters, client emails) saved as text or PDF.
- A browser, or the Claude desktop/mobile app. Web is easiest for file uploads.
- Time to prepare the rules and review test drafts. Twenty minutes gets the project built; calibration takes longer.

## Step 1: Create a Project for one type of writing

![claude.com official page screenshot](https://afroditena.github.io/mattress-checklist-android/assets/img/how-to-keep-a-consistent-writing-style-in-claude-projects/3.png)
*Screenshot of claude.com ([source](https://claude.com/pricing))*

Open Claude, click "Projects" on the left side or go straight to claude.ai/projects, then click "+ New Project" in the upper right. Name it for the *output*, not the topic - "Weekly Newsletter," "Client Case Studies," "LinkedIn Posts."

This matters more than it sounds. A single catch-all "Writing" project forces you to write vague instructions that fit everything, which is exactly how you end up with generic output. One project per format lets you get specific about length, structure, and tone.

## Step 2: Write project instructions that actually constrain Claude

Inside the project, find the instructions field (the panel is labeled for project instructions or custom instructions, depending on your version) and add your rules there. Anthropic recommends using project instructions to provide project-specific context, set guidelines for a workflow, establish requirements for a set of tasks, and define roles Claude should adopt - especially when you need Claude to hold the same context across multiple conversations in the same project.

The trick is writing rules Claude can check itself against. "Be conversational" does nothing. These do:

- **Sentence and paragraph limits.** "Paragraphs max three sentences. Vary sentence length - don't write three long ones in a row."
- **Banned words and tics.** List the words you never use. Mine would include "delve," "leverage," "in today's fast-paced world." A concrete blocklist gives you something specific to check in the draft.
- **Structural rules.** "Open with the answer, not context. No summary paragraph at the end. Subheads are sentence case."
- **Point of view and address.** "First person singular. Address the reader as 'you.' Never 'we' unless describing the company."
- **Formatting.** "Bullets only for lists of three or more parallel items. No bold inside body paragraphs."
- **A voice anchor.** One or two sentences: "Sounds like a senior colleague explaining something over coffee - confident, specific, occasionally funny, never salesy."

Keep the instructions concise and focused on context, key guidelines, and the role Claude should take, in line with [Anthropic's usage and length guidance](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/11647753-how-do-usage-and-length-limits-work). I haven't measured one page against three, so treat brevity as a documented recommendation rather than a tested result.

## Step 3: Upload real samples as project knowledge

Instructions describe your voice; samples *demonstrate* it. Add 3–5 finished pieces to the project's knowledge files. Project files are capped at 30MB each, with no limit on how many, across PDF, DOCX, CSV, TXT, HTML and more, so a handful of posts is nowhere near the ceiling.

Two rules for picking them. First, upload only work that's already in the voice you want - one off-brand piece drags the average. Second, upload finished, published versions, not drafts. If you have an internal style guide or a list of approved product terms, add that too.

Then add one line to your instructions telling Claude what to do with the files: "Before drafting, review the sample posts in project knowledge and match their rhythm, paragraph length, and level of directness."

## Step 4 (optional): Use account-level instructions or a skill for your voice

Anthropic's help center says Styles are moving to skills: custom styles are migrated to skills that start disabled, the Concise, Explanatory and Formal presets are removed, Learning becomes a skill, and the styles menu disappears once the migration is complete ([source](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/10181068-styles-are-moving-to-skills)). You enable a migrated style under Customize > Skills and activate it in a chat with a slash command in the form /{style-name}-style. If you'd rather not use skills, the same article says you can describe tone, format and approach in Instructions for Claude, which apply to all your conversations.

One behavioral difference is worth knowing before you move a style over. Skills are not always on - Anthropic's skills article explains that Claude determines which skills are relevant and loads what it needs for the task. A style applied to every turn and a skill Claude chooses to load are not the same guarantee.

This area is actively changing. In mid-2026 the plus menu still showed both Skills and Use style side by side, so check the current help center articles on [personalization](https://support.anthropic.com/en/articles/10185728-understanding-claude-s-personalization-features) and [creating custom skills](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/12512198-how-to-create-custom-skills) before relying on a specific menu path.

## Step 5: Calibrate with a test piece, then lock it in

Run one real assignment. Compare the draft to your best sample side by side and note every place you'd edit. Then, instead of fixing the draft, fix the *instructions*: turn each edit into a rule and paste it into the project.

Expect a few calibration passes. No fixed number of rounds guarantees consistency, but if you make the same correction twice, that's a rule you haven't written down yet. Treat the instructions field as a living document and reread it whenever the output drifts.

## FAQ

**Do I need a paid plan for this?**
No. Anthropic's help center says projects are available to all users, including free accounts, with a maximum of five projects on Free. Paid plans add unlimited projects and retrieval that expands knowledge base capacity.

**What's the difference between account instructions, project instructions, and styles?**

Anthropic's current personalization overview names three features - Instructions for Claude, project instructions, and skills - and assigns tone and format to skills. Instructions for Claude are account-wide, project instructions are scoped to one project, and skills shape how Claude formats and delivers responses. The three can be used independently or together.

**Will my style rules leak into my other chats?**
No. Project instructions only apply to chats within that project. Instructions for Claude apply to all your conversations, and an enabled skill is available across your account, so keep those general or switch them off when you're doing unrelated work.

**How many samples should I upload?** Three to five relevant pieces is a sensible starting point, not a tested optimum. Use writing you own or have permission to share, and don't upload confidential client material without authorization.

*Updated October 2026. This guide is built from Anthropic's current help center documentation; I did not run a controlled style benchmark.*

## My Take

I think the Project is doing most of the work here, and the style layer is doing less than people assume. Project instructions apply to every chat in the workspace by default. A skill, per Anthropic's own description, loads when Claude judges it relevant. If you want your voice enforced every single time, put it in the project instructions and treat the skill as a bonus.

My read on the Styles-to-skills migration is that it's a real downgrade for writers, even if it's an upgrade for everyone else. Skills are invoked when Claude thinks they're necessary, rather than applied to every prompt the way styles were. That's fine for a document-formatting tool. It's bad for "never write the word delve," which only works if it's on 100% of the time.

The fair point against me: skills can carry scripts, templates and reference files, which a style never could. If your voice rules come bundled with an actual process - a brief format, a fact-check pass, a publishing checklist - skills are the better container and the migration gains you something.

The part I'd actually push people on is the blocklist. Vague instructions produce vague compliance, and you can't tell whether Claude followed "be conversational." You can tell instantly whether it used a banned word. Write rules you can grade in ten seconds, or you'll never know if the setup is working.

And if you're on Free, go look at the Projects button before you believe a pricing table. Anthropic's pricing page sells "unlimited projects" as a Pro benefit in a way that reads like Free gets none at all - five is plenty for one or two formats, and that's where I'd start before paying for anything.
